title: IM SO NEW I NEED HELP
author: AlarmedAd2296
selftext: im making a duke nukem style fps using chat got hooked up to blender and Godot, but my workflow is so ass, I was making small, clearly stated tweaks, changing simple values, USING ASTRA 6.2 MEDIUM, ive probably wasted hundred if not thousands of credits/tokens so far I need help

comments.author: Ohgood9002
comments.body: Did you make any sort of plan or game design document?

comments.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
comments.body:
I spent at least 120 - 150 hours and probably more watching videos on how to make games from the perspective of a developer. In turn, it took me down many rabbit holes on art design, play mechanics, user engagement, UXI development, play testing.

And it paid off. I educated myself so my workflow wasn't "ASS" ....

I think you know you probably need to educate yourself. Are you will? I don't know.

These games will only be as good as the direction you give them. You DO NOT want AI designing shit for you. Trust me. Sometimes it's brilliant and other times it's "ASS" I personally do not trust Claude with art direction on it's own. There is where all the AI Slop comes from.

If you're not interested to go and watch those boring videos, then, your games are going to suffer.

Did watching 120 - 150+ hours of videos on video game development help me? Absolutely. I have 2 games on Steam. I worked on both in parallel over the course of 2 1/2 months. I had extensive notes on my game, from the games blue print, to art, to play mechanics, to the interface, to all aspects of making a great game, that I learned from watching videos.

I have 2 games on Steam and received my first ACH bank transfer the 2nd of Nov, this month, for just under $14,000. I bought me a 48" LG OLED C6, New KRK Studio speakers, a new external audio DAC, and I spent $6,500 on a used RTX 5090 so I could get access to that 32GB of VRAM. Yesterday for our Thanksgiven dinner, I paid someone $450 to cater our Thanksgiving dinner so we didn't have to cook. It was amazing. Here in a few days, around the 2nd or so of December, I will get another ACH bank transfer, and for Christmas, we are going to Florida for 2 weeks.

So, ask yourself, are you going to just jack around Claude and half ass it, or, do you want ot try and make real money with a real game that you put real effort into.

Good luck.

comments.author: Kindly-Sail6260
comments.body:
Brother if you never made games, I suggest you get as educated as your can learning game development since you’ll need to learn the structure of making a duke nukem like or a “boomer shooter” as that’s what that game is commonly referred to. You’re going to need to understand your engine of choice that you’re using. So if you don’t understand godot. Learn what modes, scripts, shaders, etc. find out what makes them tick and where they even are. And since it’s godot you’ll have a lot of scenes to look through and direct your AI to make sure the right things are on the right scenes. 

Some advice: The AI game dev space is quickly changing since a lot of new AI devs are recognizing that they’re extremely limited in how to make games. Most will drop like flies once their project gets out of their scope of what they’re capable of even as a game designer. So instead of panicking and finding better AI workflows that won’t work for you. Learn what it takes to make a game and try again with a fresh project of the same game you’re working. You’ll realize how much you didn’t know before.

comments.author: WhosLive
comments.body: For small value tweaks it's usually way cheaper to pull them out of code entirely, like exported variables in Godot or a single config/resource file, so you change numbers in the inspector instead of spending a prompt. A common approach is to only use the AI for actual new systems, and give it just the one script it needs plus a short note on what it does, not the whole project. Worth keeping a simple design doc with your weapon stats, enemy behavior and level rules too, so each prompt can point at it instead of re-explaining. And commit to git before every AI change so a bad edit is one revert instead of five more prompts trying to fix it.

replies.author: AlarmedAd2296
replies.body: can I have the ai pull up the inspector for me, ngl my setup hasn't touched code at all, but I built the game in chunks not all at once, its giving me great control over my ideas but idk if im wasting more doing that too

replies.author: WhosLive
replies.body: Usually the AI can't click around the editor for you, but it can add the export keyword (`@export`) to the variables you keep tweaking, and then they show up in the Inspector panel when you select that node so you edit numbers there for free. Building in chunks is actually the right call, the token waste usually comes from small value changes, not from new features. So a decent split is: AI for new systems, Inspector for tuning.

comments.author: h1soft
comments.body:
Yes, install git, and commit every time something works. When the AI breaks things (it will), you just roll back instead of spending more tokens asking it to undo its own changes.

And like someone said, don't spend prompts on number tweaks. Put speeds, damage etc. in exported variables and change them in the inspector yourself. Save the AI for actual features, one small piece at a time.

comments.author: Aaron_rowe81
comments.body: keep a tiny note of the property and its old and new value for each tweak. then you can catch an unexpected change before the next prompt builds on it.
